profile.name: Akdağmadeni halay
profile.tagline: A Cappadocian Pontic Greek halay forged in the mines of Yozgat.
profile.insight: In early 20th-century Yozgat, Pontic Greek miners who migrated to Akdağmadeni introduced a slow halay called Khalái, giving its name to the entire national dance genre of Turkey.
profile.profile: Akdağmadeni halay is a slow-paced, semi-circular folk dance that originated in the Akdağmadeni district of Yozgat Province during the early 20th century. Introduced by Pontic Greek miners migrating from the Eastern Black Sea to Central Anatolia, the dance is defined by intense bending movements, rhythmic foot strikes, and a signature six-step sequence. Executed to the music of the violin, oud, zurna, and davul, it features dancers linked together while stepping diagonally right and measuring precise toe-inward, heel-outward foot placements. Its success among surrounding Cappadocian communities turned its local refrain, Khalái, into the generic Turkish term halay for circular and line folk dances nationwide.
profile.profile_long:
Akdağmadeni halay traces its origins to the early 20th century in the Akdağmadeni district of Yozgat Province, located in Central Anatolia. During this period, Pontic Greek miners migrated from the Eastern Black Sea region to work in Akdağmadeni. These miners brought with them a distinct slow-paced, semi-circular dance known in Pontic Greek as Khalái (Χαλάι). The dance took its name from the refrain of a Turkish folk song popular among the community that accompanied the performance, indicating that these Pontic Greeks were Turkish-speaking. The term eventually caught on among neighboring communities in Cappadocia and was generalized across Turkey to describe all hand-held circular and line folk dances.

How it is danced relies on a unison semi-circular or line formation with dancers holding each other. The performance begins at a slow, deliberate pace characterized by intense bending movements and rhythmic foot strikes against the earth. Dancers begin the movement on the right foot, stepping diagonally to the right for the first three counts. On the fourth count, the dancers extend their feet toward the center of the circle. On the fifth step, they step backward with the left foot, placing the toe pointed inward and the heel outward. On the sixth step, the dancers return their feet to the position of the fourth step before repeating the entire cycle in synchronized unison.

The dance is traditionally accompanied by musical instruments including the violin, oud, zurna (a double-reed wind instrument), and davul (a large double-headed drum). The instrumentation blends the lyrical string sounds of the violin and oud with the piercing, high-volume outdoor sonorities of the zurna and davul. Performances often start at a measured, deliberate tempo before gradually accelerating as the musical phrasing intensifies.

Participants traditionally wear regional Central Anatolian attire suitable for community celebrations. The dancers form a connected chain, holding each other by the fingers, hands, or shoulders. The lead dancer at the front of the line and the trailing dancer at the end often wave a traditional handkerchief known as a mendil to direct the group and emphasize key movement counts.

While originally developed by Turkish-speaking Pontic Greek mining families as a communal expression, the dance rapidly spread to broader populations in Cappadocia and neighboring provinces such as Sivas, Çorum, and Kayseri. Each locale adapted the structure into distinct regional variants while maintaining the underlying six-step core, cementing Akdağmadeni's role in the wider lineage of Anatolian halay traditions.

sections.origins_and_history: Akdağmadeni halay emerged in the early 20th century in the Akdağmadeni district of Yozgat Province in Central Anatolia. It was developed by Pontic Greek miners who migrated to the area from the Eastern Black Sea region. Known originally in Pontic Greek as Khalái (Χαλάι), the dance took its name from the refrain of a Turkish folk song popular among these Turkish-speaking Pontic Greek miners. The style gained wide recognition across Cappadocia, where neighboring communities adopted the term to describe circular and line folk dances generally, spurring regional variants across Sivas, Çorum, and Kayseri.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a semi-circular or line formation with participants holding each other by the fingers, hands, or shoulders. Dancers execute a slow-paced sequence characterized by intense bending movements and rhythmic foot strikes. The sequence begins on the right foot, taking three steps diagonally to the right. On the fourth step, dancers extend their feet toward the center of the circle. On the fifth step, they step backward with the left foot, placing the toe inward and the heel outward. On the sixth step, they return to the position of the fourth step, repeating the cycle in unison.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is traditionally accompanied by a musical ensemble comprising the violin, oud, zurna, and davul. The music begins slowly and gradually accelerates, driving the unison footwork of the line.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed at community gatherings and festive celebrations, dancers link hands or shoulders in a line or semi-circle. The first and last dancers in the chain frequently hold and wave a mendil, a traditional handkerchief.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally performed by mining families as a social and community dance, it served as a shared cultural tradition among Pontic Greek and Anatolian communities in Yozgat.
sections.notable_figures: Hamit Zübeyir Koşay and İshak Işıtman documented the broader halay tradition in their 1932 ethnographic compilation Anadilden Derlemeler.
sections.regional_variants: Following its adoption in Akdağmadeni, variants of the dance spread to Sivas, Çorum, Kayseri, and other areas of northern Cappadocia, each establishing localized characteristics while preserving the basic footwork structure.
sections.lineage: Akdağmadeni halay belongs to the broader halay family of Anatolian circular and line dances and shares structural similarities with regional Caucasian and Middle Eastern line traditions such as Azerbaijani Yalli.

basic_steps: Extend feet toward the center of the circle (Count 4)
Step backward with left foot, placing toe inward and heel outward (Count 5)
Return left foot to the center-extended position of count 4 (Count 6)
teaching.rhythm: Slow-paced starting tempo that gradually accelerates
teaching.formation: Semi-circle or line, holding fingers, hands, or shoulders
teaching.level_notes: Requires control over deep knee bending, precise toe-inward/heel-outward foot placement, and unison group timing.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Slow rhythmic pattern featuring deliberate foot strikes, accelerating gradually
music_profile.vocal_style: Refrain singing by accompanying dancers or musicians
music_profile.musical_form: Strophic song structure with repetitive refrain sections that accelerate over time
music_profile.sound_description: A rich Central Anatolian acoustic blend featuring the resonant bowed tone of the violin and plucked oud, punctuated by the sharp, driving double-reed blast of the zurna and the booming bass rhythm of the davul drum.

movement_profile.posture: Upright torso with deep, intense knee-bending movements
movement_profile.footwork: Diagonal steps to the right followed by center extensions and backward left-foot placements with toe inward and heel outward
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Linked by fingers, hands, or shoulders; lead and end dancers hold a mendil handkerchief
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Engaged in deep flexions corresponding to rhythmic foot strikes
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Semi-circular or line formation moving along a curved spatial path
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Starts slow with heavy rhythmic strikes, building up speed continuously

signature_moves.name: Left Foot Inward Placement
signature_moves.description: Stepping backward on the left foot while angling the toe inward and the heel outward.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Low to medium level sink via intense knee bends; no jumps described
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid breaking line connection or rushing the initial slow tempo.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Underground Origins of Turkey's National Dance
episode_brief.logline: Discover how Pontic Greek miners in Yozgat created a slow, bending line dance that gave Turkey its most famous folk genre.
beats: Show the historical mining landscape of Akdağmadeni in Yozgat Province.
Demonstrate the initial slow diagonal steps to the right.
Break down the distinctive count-five foot placement (toe inward, heel outward).
Introduce the acoustic blend of violin, oud, zurna, and davul.
Perform the gradual tempo acceleration with a full line of linked dancers.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the 6-count footwork sequence in isolation
drills: Practice three diagonal steps to the right
Practice center foot extension on count 4
Practice toe-inward heel-outward placement on count 5

lesson_ladder.goal: Integrate knee bends and hold line formation with partners
drills: Execute footwork while holding fingers or shoulders in a line
Add deep knee flexions on counts 4 through 6

lesson_ladder.goal: Dance at full speed while holding mendil lead role
drills: Lead the line using mendil handkerchief cues
Maintain structural accuracy during gradual tempo acceleration

connections.name: Halay
connections.note: Akdağmadeni halay (Khalái) provided the name and early model for the wider Turkish halay genre.

connections.name: Yallı
connections.note: Shares line and circle floor patterns and similar instrumentation across Turkic/Anatolian traditions.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the 6-count sequence seated: tap right foot diagonally on 1-3, extend both feet on 4, touch left toe inward with heel outward on 5, return to center on 6.
seniors.standing_version: Perform the step sequence while holding a stable chair back for support, reducing knee-bend depth.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Maintain a steady slow tempo without acceleration; limit knee flexion angle.
seniors.counts: Counts 1 through 6 executed at a constant moderate speed.

children.game_version: Follow-the-leader chain game where the front dancer waves the mendil and speeds up the group.
children.counts: Simple 1-2-3 step, 4 reach, 5 toe-in, 6 back count.

gaps: Specific traditional musical recordings or albums dedicated exclusively to Akdağmadeni halay are not named in the sources.
